summary: Defines the Point-to-Point Protocol: how it is organized and encapsulated, and an extensible option negotiation mechanism for configuring a link. It was replaced by RFC 1661.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP is the set of rules two machines use when they are connected by a single link, such as a phone line or a serial cable. It gives each packet a two-octet field naming the network protocol inside it, so several protocols can share the link. Before any data flows, the two ends negotiate the link's settings and may check each other's identity.

questions: what is the ppp protocol field
subtitle: How two ends of a direct link agree on how to talk, check who they are, and carry several network protocols at once.

tldr.problem: A direct link between two machines has to agree on framing, on the size of packets it can carry, and on who is on the other end, and it often has to carry more than one network protocol at the same time.
tldr.mechanism: PPP defines a two-octet protocol field that says what each packet carries, a Link Control Protocol that negotiates the link's options and tests it, and a family of Network Control Protocols that configure each network-layer protocol separately.
tldr.outcome: The link goes through fixed phases, from dead through establishment, optional authentication and network configuration, to termination. RFC 1548 was obsoleted by RFC 1661.

facts.label: Encapsulation overhead
facts.value: 8 octets with the default HDLC framing

facts.label: Protocol field
facts.value: 2 octets, and all values must be odd

today: RFC 1548 is a Draft Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 1661. It was updated by RFC 1570.

sections.title: What PPP Is Made Of
sections.content:
PPP provides a standard method for transporting multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links. It is made of three main components: a method for encapsulating multi-protocol datagrams, a Link Control Protocol for establishing, configuring and testing the data-link connection, and a family of Network Control Protocols for establishing and configuring different network-layer protocols. This document defines the PPP organisation and methodology, the PPP encapsulation, and an extensible option negotiation mechanism that can negotiate a rich assortment of configuration parameters and provides additional management functions.

The encapsulation provides for multiplexing of different network-layer protocols simultaneously over the same link, and is intended to give a common solution for connecting a wide variety of hosts, bridges and routers. It has been carefully designed to retain compatibility with most commonly used supporting hardware. Only 8 additional octets are necessary to form the encapsulation when used with the default HDLC framing, and in environments where bandwidth is at a premium the encapsulation and framing may be shortened to 2 or 4 octets. To support high speed implementations the default encapsulation uses only simple fields, only one of which needs to be examined for demultiplexing, the default header and information fields fall on 32-bit boundaries, and the trailer may be padded to an arbitrary boundary.

The Link Control Protocol makes PPP portable to a wide variety of environments. It is used to automatically agree on the encapsulation format options, handle varying limits on packet sizes, authenticate the identity of its peer, determine when a link is functioning properly and when it is defunct, detect a looped-back link and other common misconfiguration errors, and terminate the link.

The Network Control Protocols exist because point-to-point links exacerbate many problems with the current family of network protocols. Assignment and management of IP addresses, which is a problem even in LAN environments, is especially difficult over circuit-switched point-to-point links such as dial-up modem servers. Each NCP manages the specific needs of its own network-layer protocol, and they are defined in companion documents.

PPP links are intended to be easy to configure. By design the standard defaults handle all common configurations; the implementor can specify improvements, which are communicated to the peer automatically without operator intervention, and the operator may explicitly configure options for the link to work in environments where it would otherwise be impossible. This self-configuration is implemented through the extensible option negotiation mechanism, in which each end of the link describes to the other its capabilities and requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Three pieces, each with its own job. The encapsulation says what is inside each packet. The Link Control Protocol sets up the link itself: it agrees the options, checks the link works, and shuts it down. The Network Control Protocols set up each network protocol separately, so IP can be configured without touching how the link behaves.

sections.title: The PPP Encapsulation
sections.content:
The PPP encapsulation is used to disambiguate multiprotocol datagrams. It requires framing to indicate the beginning and end of the encapsulation, and methods of providing framing are specified in companion documents. The encapsulation has three fields: a Protocol field, an Information field and a Padding field.

The Protocol field is two octets and its value identifies the datagram encapsulated in the Information field. It is transmitted and received most significant octet first. The structure is consistent with the ISO 3309 extension mechanism for address fields. All Protocol values MUST be odd, so the least significant bit of the least significant octet must equal 1, and all Protocol values MUST be assigned so that the least significant bit of the most significant octet equals 0. Frames received that do not comply are treated as having an unrecognised Protocol.

The ranges of the field carry meaning. Values whose first hexadecimal digit is 0 through 3 identify the network-layer protocol of specific packets, values whose first hexadecimal digit is 8 through b identify packets belonging to the associated Network Control Protocols, values whose first hexadecimal digit is 4 through 7 are used for protocols with low volume traffic that have no associated NCP, and values whose first hexadecimal digit is c through f identify packets as link-layer control protocols such as LCP. Among the assigned values are 0021 for the Internet Protocol, c021 for the Link Control Protocol, c023 for the Password Authentication Protocol and c223 for the Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol. Developers of new protocols MUST obtain a number from IANA.

The Information field is zero or more octets and holds the datagram for the protocol named in the Protocol field. The maximum length for the Information field, including Padding, is the Maximum Receive Unit, which defaults to 1500 octets; by negotiation, consenting implementations may use other values. On transmission the Information field MAY be padded with an arbitrary number of octets up to the MRU, and it is the responsibility of each protocol to distinguish padding octets from real information.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a two-octet number naming the protocol inside it, and the receiver reads that number to decide where to hand the packet. The numbering scheme is arranged so the ranges themselves say what kind of packet it is: network protocol, its control protocol, or a link control protocol.

sections.title: The Link Phases
sections.content:
To establish communications over a point-to-point link, each end of the PPP link MUST first send LCP packets to configure and test the data link. After the link has been established the peer MAY be authenticated, then PPP MUST send NCP packets to choose and configure one or more network-layer protocols, and once each of the chosen network-layer protocols has been configured, datagrams from each can be sent over the link. The link stays configured until explicit LCP or NCP packets close it down, or until an external event occurs such as an inactivity timer expiring or network administrator intervention.

The Link Dead phase is where the link necessarily begins and ends. When an external event, such as carrier detection or network administrator configuration, indicates that the physical layer is ready to be used, PPP proceeds to Link Establishment. During this phase the LCP automaton is in the Initial or Starting states, and the transition signals an Up event to the automaton.

In Link Establishment, the LCP is used to establish the connection through an exchange of Configure packets. The exchange is complete, and the LCP Opened state entered, once a Configure-Ack packet has been both sent and received. All configuration options are assumed to be at default values unless altered by the exchange. Only configuration options that are independent of particular network-layer protocols are configured by LCP; configuration of individual network-layer protocols is handled by separate NCPs later. Any non-LCP packets received during this phase MUST be silently discarded.

In the Authentication phase, on some links it may be desirable to require a peer to authenticate itself before network-layer protocol packets are exchanged. By default authentication is not mandatory, and if an implementation wants a peer to authenticate with a specific protocol it MUST negotiate the use of that protocol during Link Establishment. Authentication SHOULD take place as soon as possible after link establishment, and advancement to the Network-Layer Protocol phase MUST NOT occur until authentication has completed. If authentication fails, PPP SHOULD proceed instead to Link Termination. Any NCP or network-layer protocol packets received during this phase MUST be silently discarded.

In the Network-Layer Protocol phase, each network-layer protocol MUST be separately configured by the appropriate NCP, and each NCP MAY be Opened and Closed at any time. Once a NCP has reached the Opened state, PPP carries the corresponding network-layer protocol packets, and any such packets received when the NCP is not Opened MUST be silently discarded. The exception is that while LCP is Opened, any protocol packet unsupported by the implementation MUST be returned in a Protocol-Reject; only protocols that are supported are silently discarded. In the Link Termination phase, PPP can terminate the link at any time, because of loss of carrier, authentication failure, link quality failure, expiry of an idle timer, or administrative closing. LCP closes the link through an exchange of Terminate packets, and informs the network-layer protocols so they can take appropriate action.
sections.plainLanguage: A PPP link passes through a fixed sequence. It starts dead, comes up, negotiates its settings, may check identities, then configures each network protocol, and finally shuts down. At every stage, packets that belong to a later stage are dropped rather than processed, so nothing runs before the link is ready for it.

sections.title: The Option Negotiation Automaton
sections.content:
The option negotiation is defined by a finite-state automaton driven by events, actions and state transitions. Events include reception of external commands such as Open and Close, expiration of the Restart timer, and reception of packets from the peer. Actions include starting the Restart timer and transmitting packets to the peer.

Some types of packets are not differentiated in the automaton descriptions, because they always cause the same transitions. Configure-Naks and Configure-Rejects, Code-Rejects and Protocol-Rejects, and Echo-Requests, Echo-Replies and Discard-Requests do serve different functions later in the document, but from the automaton's point of view they behave alike.

The states are described in detail in the RFC. In the Initial state the lower layer is unavailable and no Open has occurred, and the Restart timer is not running. Starting is the Open counterpart to Initial, entered when an administrative Open has been initiated but the lower layer is still unavailable; when the lower layer becomes available, a Configure-Request is sent. In the Closed state the link is available but no Open has occurred, and on reception of Configure-Request packets a Terminate-Ack is sent. Stopped is the Open counterpart to Closed and is a junction state for link termination, configuration failure and other failure modes, combined because these potentially separate states would otherwise add little. Closing is entered when a Terminate-Request has been sent and the Restart timer is running but no Terminate-Ack has arrived.

The remaining states describe the negotiation itself: Req-Sent when a Configure-Request has been sent and no response has arrived, Ack-Received when a Configure-Request has been sent and a Configure-Ack has been received but no Configure-Request has yet been received, and Ack-Sent when a Configure-Request and a Configure-Ack have been exchanged but the peer's Configure-Request has not been received. The Opened state is reached when both ends have sent and received a Configure-Ack, and the Terminated state follows a successful termination.
sections.plainLanguage: The negotiation is written as a state machine so that both ends behave the same way in every situation, including the awkward ones such as a repeated request. The states run from initial and starting, through closed and stopped, into the three negotiation states, and finally opened or terminated.

sections.title: LCP Packets and Configuration Options
sections.content:
Every LCP packet has the same four-field header: a one-octet Code that identifies the kind of packet, a one-octet Identifier that aids in matching requests and replies, a two-octet Length giving the length of the packet including those fields, and a Data field of zero or more octets whose format depends on the Code. The assigned Code values are 1 Configure-Request, 2 Configure-Ack, 3 Configure-Nak, 4 Configure-Reject, 5 Terminate-Request, 6 Terminate-Ack, 7 Code-Reject, 8 Protocol-Reject, 9 Echo-Request, 10 Echo-Reply and 11 Discard-Request. A packet received with an invalid Code field causes a Code-Reject packet to be transmitted, while a packet with an invalid Identifier or Length field is silently discarded.

An implementation wishing to open a connection MUST transmit a packet with the Code field set to 1, Configure-Request, and the Options field filled with any desired changes to the link defaults; configuration options SHOULD NOT be included with default values. The Identifier field MUST be changed whenever the content of the Options field changes, and whenever a valid reply has been received for a previous request, though for retransmissions it MAY remain unchanged. On receipt of a Configure-Request an appropriate reply MUST be transmitted. If every option received is recognisable and all values are acceptable, the reply is a Configure-Ack carrying the same Identifier and a copy of the options, which MUST NOT be reordered or modified in any way. If every element is recognisable but some values are not acceptable, the reply is a Configure-Nak containing only the unacceptable options, with the acceptable ones filtered out. A Configure-Reject is used for options that are not recognised at all.

Configuration options allow negotiation of modifications to the default characteristics of a point-to-point link. If an option is not included in a Configure-Request, its default value is assumed. The end of the list is indicated by the length of the LCP packet. Each option has a one-octet Type, a one-octet Length covering the Type, Length and Data fields, and a Data field. The option types defined here are 1 Maximum-Receive-Unit, 2 Async-Control-Character-Map, 3 Authentication-Protocol, 4 Quality-Protocol, 5 Magic-Number, 6 RESERVED, 7 Protocol-Field-Compression and 8 Address-and-Control-Field-Compression.
sections.plainLanguage: Every control packet has the same small header, and the Code says which of eleven kinds it is. The options ride in the data field as a list of type-and-length entries. The answer to a request says what the other end thinks: accept everything, accept some but suggest different values for the rest, or refuse the ones it does not recognise.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's own security considerations are brief. It says security issues are discussed in the sections concerning the Authentication Phase, the Close event and the Authentication-Protocol Configuration Option, and that further discussion is in a companion document entitled PPP Authentication Protocols.

Those parts of the document do say that an implementation which wants a peer to authenticate with a specific protocol MUST negotiate the use of that protocol during Link Establishment, and that advancement from the Authentication phase to the Network-Layer Protocol phase MUST NOT occur until authentication has completed. If authentication fails, PPP SHOULD proceed to the Link Termination phase, and the sender of a Terminate-Request SHOULD disconnect after receiving a Terminate-Ack or after the Restart counter expires, which the RFC singles out as particularly important in the case of an authentication failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The security discussion is short and mostly points elsewhere. The parts that matter here are the rule that the link does not carry network traffic until authentication has finished, and the rule that a failed authentication leads to the link being shut down rather than left open.

items.label: Configure-Request
items.desc: Proposes the link options the sender wants.

items.label: Configure-Ack
items.desc: Accepts every option in the request.

items.label: Configure-Nak
items.desc: Accepts the options but suggests different values for some.

items.label: Configure-Reject
items.desc: Refuses options it does not recognise.

items.label: Protocol-Reject
items.desc: Reports a protocol the implementation does not support.

items.label: Echo-Request
items.desc: Tests that the link is working.

items.label: Discard-Request
items.desc: Tests the link by sending a packet that is discarded.
